measures.title: The Cook County Millionaire Amendment for Property Tax Relief and Education
measures.question: Shall Illinois adopt the Millionaire Amendment for Property Tax Relief and Education, which would enact a 3% income tax surcharge only on millionaires and use 50% of this new revenue to provide property tax relief for residential and commercial taxpayers and 50% to improve state funding for public education?
measures.plain: Advisory: it changes no law by itself. The Cook County Board put it on every county ballot in July to gauge support for a statewide constitutional amendment (a proposal in the Illinois House, backed by House Speaker Welch and Mayor Johnson) adding a 3% surcharge on income over $1 million; Illinois’ constitution requires a flat income tax, so a real change would need a statewide vote. Supporters say it would raise about $4 billion a year from roughly 41,000 taxpayers for property-tax relief and schools; opponents say it would push high earners and employers out of the state.

measures.title: Restart Chicago Gunshot Detection
measures.question: Should the City of Chicago restart the use of gunshot detection technology that informs first responders when gunshots are detected?
measures.plain: Advisory. Chicago ended its ShotSpotter contract in September 2024 after Mayor Johnson questioned the system’s accuracy and cost; a replacement has been promised but not chosen. Ald. Marty Quinn (13th), a ShotSpotter supporter, got this question onto the ballot to put voters on record. A “yes” signals the city should bring gunshot-detection sensors back; a “no” that it should stay without them.

measures.title: Permanent Chicago Festival Space
measures.question: Should Chicago develop a permanent festival and outdoor event space for large-scale events?
measures.plain: Advisory. Lollapalooza in Grant Park, Riot Fest in Douglass Park and other festivals close public parks for weeks and leave damage behind. Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) proposed asking whether the city should build a permanent fairgrounds for big events instead; there is no site or cost yet. A “yes” tells the city to pursue one.

measures.title: Chicago Cost Recovery from Midway Blitz
measures.question: Shall the City of Chicago pursue all lawful means to recover financial compensation from the federal government for the costs and economic harm caused by the Donald Trump administration's violent, militarized ICE operations, including the Midway Blitz operation led by Greg Bovino, to recover lost tax revenue, public safety response costs, and services provided to residents and families affected by those operations?
measures.plain: Advisory, backed by Mayor Johnson. “Operation Midway Blitz” was the federal immigration enforcement surge in Chicago in fall 2025, with more than 3,800 people detained; a University of Illinois Chicago study put the loss to immigrant business corridors above $1 billion. A “yes” says the city should try, in court or otherwise, to make the federal government pay for its costs and lost revenue; how it would is not spelled out.

measures.title: ADVISORY QUESTION REGARDING MILLIONAIRES SURCHARGE
measures.question: Shall Illinois use revenue from a surcharge on millionaires to increase funding to public schools?
measures.plain: Advisory, from the Chicago Board of Education, and broader than the county’s question on the same idea: it asks only whether money from a tax surcharge on millionaires should go to public schools. The school board added it in August, with the vacant-property question below, to show support for new school funding.

measures.title: ADVISORY QUESTION REGARDING CHICAGO LAND OWNERS
measures.question: Should the City of Chicago require owners of long-term vacant or undeveloped commercial or investment properties to pay an additional annual charge that would support Chicago Public Schools?
measures.plain: Advisory, from the Chicago Board of Education. It asks whether owners of commercial or investment property left vacant or undeveloped for a long time should pay an extra yearly charge, with the money going to Chicago Public Schools. Board members split: some said it would push owners to build and fund schools, others doubted it could be enforced fairly.

measures.title: Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services
measures.question: Shall there be established, to serve the territory commonly described on this ballot or notice of this question, a Mid- Northside Expanded Mental Health Services Program, to provide direct free mental health services for any resident of the territory who needs assistance in overcoming or coping with mental or emotional disorders, where such program will be funded through an increase of not more than .025% of the equalized assessed valuation of all properties within the boundaries of the territory?

scope.name: Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services Program Area

measures.plain: Binding. Under Illinois’ Community Expanded Mental Health Services Act, residents of an area can petition to create a program offering free mental-health care to anyone living there, paid for by a small property-tax levy (capped at 0.025% of the area’s equalized assessed value) and run by a locally elected governing commission. Several Chicago neighborhoods have voted such programs in since 2012. A “yes” creates one for the area named on your ballot.

measures.title: 2027 Property Tax Extension - Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services
measures.question: Under the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, may an aggregate extension not to exceed $1,300,000 be made for the Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services Program for the 2027 levy year?

scope.name: Mid-Northside Expanded Mental Health Services Program Area

measures.plain: Binding, and paired with the question above it: if the program is created, this sets how much property tax it may collect for 2027 (the dollar cap in the question, spread over the area’s property owners). A “no” here with a “yes” above would leave the program without that budget.

measures.title: Far Southwest Side Expanded Mental Health Services
measures.question: Shall there be established, to serve the territory commonly described on this ballot or notice of this question, an Far Southwest Side Expanded Mental Health Services Program, to provide direct free mental health services for any resident of the territory who needs assistance in overcoming or coping with mental or emotional disorders, where such program will be funded through an increase of not more than .025% of the equalized assessed valuation of all properties within the boundaries of the territory?

scope.name: Far Southwest Side Expanded Mental Health Services Program Area

measures.plain: Binding. Under Illinois’ Community Expanded Mental Health Services Act, residents of an area can petition to create a program offering free mental-health care to anyone living there, paid for by a small property-tax levy (capped at 0.025% of the area’s equalized assessed value) and run by a locally elected governing commission. Several Chicago neighborhoods have voted such programs in since 2012. A “yes” creates one for the area named on your ballot.

measures.title: 2027 Property Tax Extension - Far Southwest Side Expanded Mental Health Services
measures.question: Under the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, may an aggregate extension not to exceed $900,000 be made for the Far Southwest Side Expanded Mental Health Services Program for the 2027 levy year?

scope.name: Far Southwest Side Expanded Mental Health Services Program Area

measures.title: Jesse Jackson Monument Statue
measures.question: through referendum that to become a city ordinance supported by the city do hereby petition that the question, should at least a life-size statue of the likeness of Jesse Lewis Jackson Sr. sitting on a monument to be placed in the median at approximately 4946 South Drexel, Chicago Illinois be a public policy to place on the ballot and submitted to the voters of the fourth (4th) ward for their approval or disapproval by referendum at the General Election to be held on November 3rd 2026. This initiative is to become realized by November 2027. This proposal should give homage to a great American Patriot and a token symbol of America's appreciation.
measures.plain: Advisory, by petition in the 4th Ward. It asks whether the city should place a life-size statue of the Rev. Jesse L. Jackson Sr., the civil-rights leader and founder of Rainbow PUSH who died in February 2026, in the median near the organization’s Kenwood headquarters. A “yes” tells the alderperson and the city to pursue it.

measures.title: Shared Housing Limits in 26th Ward
measures.question: Shall new shared housing units be limited in the 26th Ward to help address Chicago’s severe rental housing shortage?
measures.plain: Advisory, by petition in the 26th Ward. Chicago’s shared-housing ordinance already lets precincts vote to restrict short-term rentals (Airbnb-style listings); this asks whether the whole ward should limit new ones, on the argument that they take apartments off the long-term rental market.

measures.title: Chicago Lakefront National Park
measures.question: Shall the City of Chicago support the nomination of a Chicago Lakefront National Park, consisting of all of Chicago's park and public lands adjacent to Lake Michigan including their harbors, lagoons, and inlets?
measures.plain: Advisory, by petition. A campaign wants Chicago’s lakefront parks, harbors and lagoons nominated as a unit of the National Park Service; a national park would be designated by Congress. A “yes” says the city should support the nomination.

measures.title: Ensure Remediation of Former South Works Site
measures.question: Shall governmental bodies in Illinois ensure the complete and transparent remediation of the former South Works site?
measures.plain: Advisory, by petition in the 7th and 10th Wards. The former U.S. Steel South Works site on the Southeast Side lakefront, vacant since 1992, is the planned home of the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park. Neighbors (organized as Southside Together) want a guarantee that the soil and slag there are fully cleaned up, with the results made public, before anything is built. The Board of Elections threw out an earlier, multi-part version in March; this and the question below are the single-topic versions.

measures.title: Government support for Quantum Facility and Data Center at Former South Works Site
measures.question: Shall governmental bodies in Illinois spend an estimated $1 billion of taxpayer money to support a quantum facility and data center on the former South Works site?
measures.plain: Advisory, by petition in the 7th and 10th Wards. The state has pledged public money for the quantum campus at the former South Works site, anchored by PsiQuantum, with a data center alongside. The question asks whether governments should spend an estimated $1 billion of taxpayer money on it. Supporters point to jobs and investment; neighbors who petitioned for this question want the land cleaned up and used for the community instead.

measures.title: 500+ employee Corporate Tax for Youth Jobs and Social Services
measures.question: Shall our Alderperson vote to pass a tax on big corporations that have 500 or more employees (would not apply to grocery stores or non profits), in order to fund youth jobs, public mental healthcare, and violence prevention services.
measures.plain: Advisory, by petition in a handful of precincts. During the 2026 city budget fight, Mayor Johnson proposed a “head tax” of $33 per employee on companies with 500 or more workers (about 175 firms, grocery stores and nonprofits excluded) to fund youth jobs, mental-health care and violence prevention; the City Council did not adopt it. A “yes” asks your alderperson to vote for such a tax.

measures.title: Continue to prohibit Status of retail alcohol sales in Ward 21 Precinct 10
measures.question: Shall the prohibition of the sale at retail of alcoholic liquor be continued in the 10th Precinct of the 21st Ward of the City of Chicago (as such precinct existed as of the last general election)?
measures.plain: Binding, under Illinois’ local-option law, and only for this precinct, which has voted itself “dry.” A “yes” keeps the ban on stores and bars selling alcohol there; a “no” lifts it.
